[0] everyday_reading (E): In algebra a variable is an unknown that keeps one value throughout an equation (x in x = 2y), and the 'box' metaphor suggests it can hold several things. In Java a variable is a named storage location holding exactly one value at a time, and that value changes as statements run.
[1] misconception (M) -> VariablesHoldObjects: wrong rule: a reference variable holds the whole object, not a reference. Right rule: A reference variable holds only a reference to the object, which is stored separately.
[2] misconception (M) -> MultiValueVariable: wrong rule: A variable can contain more than one value. Right rule: A variable holds exactly one value at a time; assigning a new value replaces the old one.
[3] misconception (M) -> VariableRolesInferred: wrong rule: The computer recognises that one variable plays two roles, e.g. input value and running total, and keeps the values apart; it knows which variable is the counter and which the sum. Right rule: A variable holds one value at a time; each role (input, counter, running total) needs its own variable and explicit update.
[4] misconception (M) -> VariableKeepsOldValue: wrong rule: A variable keeps its first value after a new assignment (the static model). Right rule: Each assignment or read replaces the variable's current value.
[5] inconsistent_trace (T) -> VariablesHoldObjects: Points to LT (a read gives the current value, and each assignment replaces it). Applied unevenly, a student updates the value after some assignments but keeps the first value after others, or switches between a memory model and an equation model across tasks (y = x - y read as x = 2y). (here mixing in: "a reference variable holds the whole object, not a reference")
[6] misconception (M) -> LocalVarOutsideScope: wrong rule: A variable declared inside a block can be used anywhere in the program, like a global. Right rule: A local variable exists only from its declaration to the end of its block.
[7] misconception (M) -> LoopBodyScopeImpliesLoopLifetime: wrong rule: a variable declared in the loop body lives across all iterations. Right rule: A variable declared inside the body is created anew on every pass and does not keep the previous pass's value.
[8] misconception (M) -> NameGivesMeaning: wrong rule: Naming a variable max (or average) makes it hold the largest value (or the average) without code that computes it. Right rule: A name only labels the variable for human readers; only the statements that assign to it decide its value.
[9] misconception (M) -> VariablesHoldExpressions: wrong rule: = stores the expression itself, not its computed value. Right rule: y = x + k; stores the value that x + k has at that moment, so later changes to x do not change y.
[10] misconception (M) -> AnyValueInAnyVariable: wrong rule: A variable declared int can hold 2.5 or "hi"; the type is only a label. Right rule: A data type is a set of values and a set of operations defined on them, so an int variable holds only int values.
[11] misconception (M) -> LocalVariablesAutoInitialized: wrong rule: local variables get a default value on their own. Right rule: A local variable has no value until it is assigned, and using it before then does not compile.
[12] misconception (M) -> NoReservedWords: wrong rule: keywords may be reused as identifiers. Right rule: Keywords are reserved by Java and cannot be used as variable names.
[13] misconception (M) -> DeclaredVariableHasNoMemory: wrong rule: int x; without a value sets aside no memory; the variable only exists once something is assigned. Right rule: A declaration creates the variable (its storage) with its type; assignment later puts a value in it.
[14] misconception (M) -> RereadIntoVariableInvalid: wrong rule: Reading a second input value into a variable that already holds one is an error, so the program cannot run. Right rule: A later read simply overwrites the variable's current value.
[15] misconception (M) -> ArrayElementNotVariable: wrong rule: An array element a[i] is not a variable, so it cannot be read into directly or used inside another index, as in a[a[i]]. Right rule: Each element a[i] is a variable of the element type and can be used anywhere a variable of that type can, including as an index.

[0] names_the_element (N): Variable: a name that refers to a typed storage location holding one data-type value.
[1] states_the_rule (S): A variable must be declared with a type before use. It always holds a value of that type, must be assigned before it is read, and can be used only within its scope (from its declaration to the end of the enclosing block).

[0] line_by_line_trace (LT): Each time execution reaches an expression that uses the variable, its current value is fetched at that moment. An assignment to it takes effect only after its right-hand side has been fully evaluated.
[1] output_prediction (OP): A variable in an expression yields the value most recently assigned to it, with its declared type. After int a = 5; int b = a; a = 3;, a is 3 and b is 5.
[2] one_step_execution (OS): Only an assignment or an input read into the variable changes it, and it changes only that variable, replacing the old value. Other variables keep their values.

[0] relation_to_neighbour (R): Literals commonly give variables their values, and the literal's type must fit the variable's type (int x = 1.1; is rejected).
[1] relation_to_neighbour (R): Assignment is the only statement that changes a variable, and its left-hand side must be a single variable.
[2] relation_to_neighbour (R): A variable name is itself an expression whose value is the variable's current value, and it combines with operators into larger expressions.
[3] relation_to_neighbour (R): Each variable is named by an identifier, which must be legal and unique within the variable's scope.
[4] relation_to_neighbour (R): A variable's name should describe what it holds (lowerCamelCase), but the name has no effect on its value.
[5] relation_to_neighbour (R): The current values of all variables make up the program's state. A trace records each variable's value after each statement.
[6] purpose_of_the_whole (P): Variables keep track of values that change as a computation unfolds, each in one role (Sajaniemi): fixed value, stepper, most-recent holder, gatherer (running total), most-wanted holder, follower, one-way flag or temporary.

[0] predict_a_change (C) -> VariablesHoldObjects: Renaming a variable consistently keeps behavior. Reordering statements that write and read it changes results (a = b; b = a; is not a swap). Moving its declaration into a loop body narrows its scope and resets it on every pass.
[1] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: Every variable must be declared (with a type) before use and referred to by exactly the declared name, inside its scope. Kind: compile-time. Trigger class: Use of a name that was never declared, was declared under another name, or is used outside the block where it was declared: 'cannot find symbol' (one missing declaration can produce several errors).
[2] transfer_to_a_new_program (X): Use a variable when a value must be remembered, changes during the computation, or deserves a name as an intermediate result. Use a final constant for a value that never changes, and an array when many values of one type must all be kept.
[3] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: A local variable must be assigned before it is read. Kind: compile-time. Trigger class: A read on a path where no assignment has happened (declared without initializer, or assigned only inside an if or loop): 'variable might not have been initialized'.
[4] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: A variable can be used only inside its scope. Kind: compile-time. Trigger class: Using a variable after the block, loop body or for header where it was declared has ended: 'cannot find symbol'.
[5] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: One variable holds one value, so each role needs its own variable. Kind: silent logic error. Trigger class: Reusing the same variable as both input value and running total (or counter): the earlier value is overwritten.

Every variable is named by an identifier that follows the naming rules.
A variable of type t is given a value of type t, often written as a literal.
Assignment needs a declared variable on its left side to store the computed value into.
An expression can be a literal, a variable, or operations on them; we compute with a variable by using its name in an expression.
Each variable gets a name; the convention says the name should describe what the variable holds.
Without arrays, a program's state is the values of its variables plus the next statement to run.
